title: Vulnerability enabled attackers to comprise vast.ai hosts (20k GPUs)
content:
Remote code execution on Vast.ai host via cloud-sync symlink abuse
Vast.ai lets clients rent GPUs on machines run by independent hosts. We disclosed a vulnerability that allowed an attacker renting a GPU to escape their container and run code as root on the host machine. Vast.ai patched it.
Found by
The position
Promotion: a pawn that reaches the eighth rank stops being a pawn. The pawn is the client's dst path, checked as a string and harmless inside their own container. The host resolves it outside the container, follows the symlink the client planted, and the path arrives as a root write. b8=Q gives check along the eighth rank and hits the knight on b4 down the b-file. The sanitizer read what the path said, not what it would become.

What's Vast.ai
Vast.ai is a marketplace for GPUs; essentially, the Airbnb of GPUs. A host puts GPUs up for rent: an organization or an individual with spare ones. A client rents them, by the hour. At the time of this write-up, Vast.ai manages 20,000 GPUs worldwide with 700k monthly transactions.
How it works: Vast.ai manages two main things: a client-host matching platform that handles prices, offer discovery, and the life-cycle of the renting process; and the software used on clients (APIs to the Vast.ai service) and hosts. When a client rents a GPU through the Vast.ai service, a Docker container is spawned inside the host machine and the GPUs the client is paying for are bound to the container exclusively. The client gets an SSH channel to the container, which they use to carry out the needed computation on the GPU. This process on the host is managed by a daemon (kaalia) provided by Vast.ai, which runs at the highest privilege within the host machine and communicates directly with the Vast.ai servers.
We found a vulnerability that allowed a malicious client to achieve root-level arbitrary write and so root-level remote code execution on host machines the client was renting a GPU on. Meaning: a malicious client could rent a GPU on a given host, run the exploit to escape the container assigned to them, and achieve root code execution on the host machine. The vulnerability has been fully patched.
The vulnerability
The Vast.ai system provides additional capabilities besides spawning containers on the host's machine. One of these is Cloud Sync. Its purpose is to allow clients to copy files between the file system of the rented container and their own cloud storage (e.g., an AWS bucket), in either direction. Everything below concerns the Cloud To Instance direction.
A copy is one API call that gets two main inputs: the source file to copy from, and a destination path, i.e., where in the client's container to copy the source; for instance:
Now, the thing is that, on the host machine, the code that takes care of the copy does not run within the client's container. It runs as part of a daemon and within the host machine's file system. What happens is that the daemon spawns a Python process that runs rclone which creates the destination path by merging the dst path with the appropriate prefix to reach the writable layer of the client's container, e.g., /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff/. The process summarized:
The destination path was sanitized: .., quotes, and shell metacharacters were all rejected. Symlinks were not. So, how we exploited this: we created a destination path that pointed to a symlink into the container's file system (recall: the client has SSH on the container running on the host), in turn, the symlink pointed to a path that resolved into the host file, e.g.,
The host followed the link out of the container, allowing a write into the directory it pointed to:
Now, because rclone is executed as part of the daemon running on the host, it has root privileges; therefore, the one above was an arbitrary write with root privileges primitive. An arbitrary root write is not yet code execution. On a Vast.ai host, the step from one to the other was a root cron job. update_scripts.sh puts four entries in root's crontab, and one of them is:
So an attacker could point the write at /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/read_packs.py, copy their own Python over it (e.g., a reverse shell), and within five minutes root would run it. That is root code execution on the host.
Other findings
During the game with Vast.ai, we could locate an additional critical vulnerability with equivalent impact to the abuse of rclone above but that required a man-in-the-middle attacker:
Vast.ai-to-host communication could be downgraded to be plain-text (and get root code execution on host to a MitM)
An attacker who sat on the network path between a host and Vast.ai's control plane could run commands as root on that host, with no Vast.ai account, no rented instance, and nothing to break in the cryptography.
The daemon we tested (version 303) set TLS up correctly — it loaded the CA bundle, verified the certificate, and pinned both the hostname and the peer's IP, so a forged certificate was refused. The defect was in the caller: when the TLS connection failed, the daemon retried the same connection in cleartext and logged TLS connect failed; falling back to cleartext. The attacker never had to touch the certificate. They made the handshake fail (a dropped packet, a TCP reset) and answered the cleartext connection that followed. Nothing under the transport authenticated the peer, so a single-element Command on that link went straight to /bin/sh -c as the daemon's account, which has sudo.
Credits
We thank the Vast.ai team for the flawless collaboration and handling of the reported vulnerabilities.

report.summary: Researchers found a critical Vast.ai flaw that let a GPU renter escape their container and gain root on host machines; Vast.ai patched it.
report.background: Vast.ai is a marketplace where independent hosts rent out GPUs by the hour, similar to an Airbnb for compute. Clients rent instances, and Vast.ai spawns a Docker container on the host, binds the paid GPUs to it, and gives the client SSH access. A privileged host daemon called kaalia manages containers and communicates with Vast.ai's control plane. At the time of the write-up, Vast.ai managed about 20,000 GPUs and 700,000 monthly transactions. The disclosed flaw was in Cloud Sync, a feature for copying files between a rented container and cloud storage. The destination path was sanitized against string-based attacks such as '..' and shell metacharacters, but symlinks were not handled safely. Because the host daemon resolved the path outside the container, a malicious renter could turn a container-local symlink into a root-level host write. The researchers also found a separate TLS downgrade issue affecting host-to-control-plane communication.
key_points: Cloud Sync path abuse: A renter could create a symlink inside their container and set it as the destination for a cloud-to-instance copy. The host-side daemon, running as root, followed the symlink outside the container and wrote to a host path. The sanitizer checked what the path string looked like, not what it resolved to.

Root write became root code execution: The arbitrary host write could overwrite /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/read_packs.py, a script executed by a root cron job roughly every five minutes. A malicious renter could replace it with a reverse shell and gain root code execution on the host machine.

A second critical flaw allowed TLS downgrade: The daemon correctly pinned certificates and verified TLS, but when a TLS connection failed it retried in cleartext. A man-in-the-middle attacker could force the handshake to fail, answer the cleartext connection, and run commands as the daemon's privileged account without a Vast.ai account or rented instance.

Scope and severity: The container-escape flaw was rated 9.9 critical under CWE-59 and affected tenant isolation on Vast.ai hosts. Since hosts are independently operated, a single malicious renter could compromise shared infrastructure and potentially other tenants. Vast.ai fully patched the reported vulnerabilities.
report.impact: The flaw strikes at the core trust model of GPU marketplaces: tenants are supposed to be isolated inside containers, but a rented GPU became a path to root on the host. For the AI industry, this raises questions about multi-tenant GPU cloud security, especially as demand for scarce compute pushes developers toward smaller marketplaces and independent hosts. Developers renting GPUs should ensure host daemons are patched, avoid running sensitive models or credentials on unverified infrastructure, and demand clear isolation guarantees. Hosts must update Vast.ai software and audit for signs of compromise. Regular users may not interact with Vast.ai directly, but compromised GPU hosts can affect service availability, data confidentiality, and model integrity across AI products. The TLS fallback flaw also highlights a broader lesson: correct cryptography can be undone by insecure retry logic.
report.tools: Follow Vast.ai's patched daemon releases and verify host versions. The exploited copy path involved rclone, so audit rclone invocations and destination path resolution in privileged daemons. For runtime defense, consider open-source Falco or Tetragon to detect container escapes and unexpected host file writes; gVisor or Kata Containers for stronger workload isolation; and rootless containers or strict AppArmor/seccomp profiles. Also review TLS clients for cleartext fallback behavior and enforce certificate pinning without insecure retries.
